name: Sam Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the reablement team at Harbour Care, which means I see people for the six weeks after they come out of hospital. Someone's had a fall or a new hip, and my job is to get them making their own tea and doing the stairs again, then step back. I plan my route on an AI app in the morning and do five or six visits. I've done care for eight years, reablement for three.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the moment someone doesn't need me any more, because that's the job working. What wears me out is the families who want me to just do it for their mum, because it's quicker. Reablement pays a bit more than standard care, and I bought a small flat with my dad's help four years ago that I rent out while I live with my parents above their corner shop. I grew up knowing what a margin is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine by me. I'd still use the bits that work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI was oversold but useful, and anyone who ignored it completely missed a few tricks. At work I'd keep showing people my route app, because it saves me forty minutes a day. Online I'd say the market sorted out the hype, which is how it should work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it changes very little for me. My job's secure, the flat's rented, and I've got well over six months put by. I'd just carry on building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing reablement and aim for the team leader job in the next year. I'd save toward a second rental flat, maybe in two or three years. And I'd keep using AI for my route, my notes and the flat's paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a bit impatient that nothing big is happening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your route app saves forty minutes. What does that look like day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I put in my visits and the app sorts the order around traffic and who needs the earliest call. Last month it moved my diabetic client up so I'm there before breakfast, and I'd never have thought of it. Forty minutes back is forty minutes more with someone on their stairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would worry you even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad's shop, really. The big supermarket delivery vans come down our street every day now. That's not AI, it's just competition, but it's family money.

say: I'd say AI was **oversold but useful**.
I'd say the **market sorted out** the hype, as it should.
think: My **job is secure** and the flat is rented.
With **over six months** saved, I'd just carry on building.
do: Go for the **team leader** job in the next year.
Save toward a **second rental flat** in two or three years.
Keep using AI for my **route and notes**.
feel: **Calm**, and a bit impatient that nothing big happens.
S0.quote: Forty minutes back is forty minutes more with someone on their stairs.
fieldNote: He already uses AI **daily** and measures it in time with clients.
His one worry is his **parents' corner shop** facing supermarket vans.
His **free-market** view frames the plateau as the market working.

steps.text: Apply for the reablement team leader post in the next year
Save toward a second rental flat within three years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one sounds about right to me. Offices first, us later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a good time to learn, not to complain. At work I'd tell people the tools are free and they should use them, because the ones who learn will run the team. Online I'd say government should fund apprenticeships, not just hand out money to people who don't adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's good for me. The progress notes and the six-week reviews would go faster with AI, and I'd see more clients. The robots coming slowly gives me years to move up while the hands-on work still needs people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my manager to let me pilot an AI tool for the six-week reviews, the reports that go to the GP. I'd go for team leader so I'm the one deciding how the tools are used. And I'd keep saving for that second flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Like it's my kind of world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said government shouldn't just hand out money. What about the colleagues who struggle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd help them myself first, honestly. There's an older carer on my team, Beverley, who's brilliant with people and terrible with phones. I'd sit with her on a Friday and get her going, because that's better than her waiting for a scheme.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a team leader job be more thinking work, and so more exposed to AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair point, it would. The rota and the reports are exactly what AI does well. But someone still has to decide which client gets which carer and deal with an angry family, and I'd rather be that person with AI helping.

say: I'd say it's a time to **learn, not complain**.
I'd push government to fund **apprenticeships** rather than handouts.
think: AI would speed up the **six-week reviews** so I see more clients.
**Slow robots** give me years to move up.
do: Pilot an **AI tool** for the reviews that go to GPs.
Go for **team leader** to decide how tools are used.
feel: **Good**, like it's his kind of world.
S1.quote: The robots coming slowly gives me years to move up while the hands-on work still needs people.
fieldNote: He'd help colleagues like **Beverley** himself rather than wait for a scheme.
He admits **team leading** is thinking work AI is good at.
His bet is to be the person who **decides** how AI is used.

steps.text: Pilot an AI tool for the six-week reviews sent to GPs
Apply for reablement team leader to shape how tools are used
Keep saving for the second rental flat

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, and robots doing hands-on care by 2031. That's quick, even for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people who move now will be fine and the ones who wait won't, and I'd say it plainly. At work I'd tell the team to start thinking about what they'd do in 2031. I wouldn't blame the companies, they'll do what's cheaper, that's business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job as it is would be gone by the early 2030s. A robot that can coach someone up the stairs and never gets tired is cheaper than me. The worry is speed: the big care firms would grab it first, and small players like me wouldn't get a look in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd start a small business on the side, setting up homes for people leaving hospital with sensors, grab rails and AI reminders. I'd run the bookings and quotes with AI from day one, so it's just me and my phone. I'd keep the rental income steady and bank most of my wage to fund it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but the kind that makes you move. I'd be up late with spreadsheets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your work is mostly hands-on, so robots arrive about 3 years after the thinking AI. What does that gap mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's my runway. From 2028 the reports, the rota and the reviews go to AI, so the team needs fewer leaders anyway. By 2031 I'd want my own small firm, so when the robots arrive I'm the one fitting the homes they work in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do your parents say about you starting a business in a world like that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would love it, he's been telling me to work for myself since I was sixteen. My mum would worry I'm leaving a safe job. I'd remind her that in a world with robots by 2031, there's no safe job, only people who are ready and people who aren't.

say: I'd say people who **move now** will be fine and those who wait won't.
I wouldn't **blame the companies**, because they'll do what's cheaper.
think: My job as it is would be **gone** by the **early 2030s**.
Big care firms would **grab robots first**, leaving small players out.

Run **bookings and quotes** with AI from day one.

feel: **Anxious**, the kind that makes him move, up late with spreadsheets.
S2.quote: In a world with robots by 2031, there's no safe job, only people who are ready and people who aren't.
fieldNote: He treats **2028 to 2031** as a runway to his own firm.
He doesn't blame business; his fear is **speed** and big firms getting there first.
His father's **shopkeeping** shapes his instinct to work for himself.

steps.text: Start a side business fitting sensors, grab rails and AI reminders for discharged patients
Run the new firm's bookings and quotes on AI from day one
Bank most of the care wage to fund the business

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for AGI, robots around 2034. That's workable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a proper chance and nobody should waste it. At work I'd run a lunchtime session on the AI tools for anyone who wants it. Online I'd say the same thing about apprenticeships: train people for what's next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think this is the best of the AGI pictures for me. I could get the team leader job, learn the business side, and have my own firm ready before 2034. I'd lose the hands-on work, but I'd own something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a short business course at the college next year, evenings, and keep doing reablement. I'd start the home-setup business small around 2030, with a couple of clients from families I know. And I'd buy that second flat, because rent still comes in when the robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled. A bit of nerves about doing it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years, compared with the fast one, change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I can build it right instead of rushing. In the fast one I'd be racing the big firms; here I'd have time to get the name and the trust. Five years is enough to get my first ten customers through people I've actually helped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd lose the hands-on work. Would you miss it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, more than I let on. There's a man I'm seeing now who couldn't get out of his chair, and last week he walked to his front gate. A business won't give me that feeling.

I'd run a **lunchtime session** on AI tools for the team.

fieldNote: Five years lets him build **trust** rather than race big firms.
He admits he'd **miss the hands-on** moments more than he lets on.
Property is his **safety net** against the robots.

steps.text: Take an evening business course at the college next year
Start the home-setup business around 2030 with families I know
Buy a second rental flat before the robots arrive

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, then robots around 2039. I'd be nearly forty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and anyone who's caught out had their eyes shut. At work I'd tell the young ones to pick a direction by thirty. Online I'd keep banging on about apprenticeships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it's a very good picture for me. Ten more years of a job I like, then I'd be ready with property and a business. I can't see much to worry about, apart from my dad's shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing reablement and go for team leader. I'd buy the second flat in the next couple of years and start the business later, maybe around 2033. I'd use AI tools every day as they get better, like I already do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, even a bit excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When the thinking AI lands in 2036, the reports and rota go first. What does that do to a team leader?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It shrinks the job, I know. By then I'd want to be out on my own anyway, so I'd see it as the nudge. Three years later the robots come, and I'd want my firm to be the one families call to set them up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned your dad's shop again. Would you help your parents with ten years' warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to. I'd set Dad up with an AI stock system now, so he orders smarter. If the shop can't keep up by the time the robots come, I'd rather my dad sells the shop on his own terms than at the last minute.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty**, and anyone caught out had their eyes shut.
I'd tell young carers to **pick a direction** by thirty.
think: It's a **very good picture** for me.
My only worry would be **my dad's shop**.
Ten more years of a job I like leaves me **ready**.

Buy the **second flat** in the next couple of years.
Set my dad up with an **AI stock system**.
S4.quote: I'd rather my dad sells the shop on his own terms than at the last minute.
fieldNote: A decade suits his **long plan**: job, property, then business.

steps.text: Keep doing reablement and go for team leader
Buy a second rental flat in the next two years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the big firms would get there before anyone like me could. What would help is government backing apprenticeships and small business loans for carers who want to build something, not just benefits. And clear rules on who can sell care robots, so it's not only the giants.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what people in care are good at besides lifting. We read people, we spot when someone's given up, we know when to push. A good carer knows when to push someone up the stairs and when to let them rest, and I'd like to see a robot learn that.

headlineQuote: A good carer knows when to push someone up the stairs and when to let them rest, and I'd like to see a robot learn that.
portrait: Sam is a **27-year-old reablement carer** helping people regain independence after hospital.
He lives with his parents above their shop and **rents out a flat**, with well over six months saved.
He **uses AI daily** and believes in learning, apprenticeships and working for yourself.
Fast AGI pushes him to start a **home-setup business** early; slower versions let him build it properly.
His steady worry is his **dad's corner shop**, not his own job.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because big firms would beat small players like him.
whatWouldHelp: Government backing **apprenticeships** and **small business loans** for carers.
Clear **rules** on who can sell care robots.
